study.title: Ezekiel 45 - Holy Land, righteousness in the measures and feasts of purification
study.overview: Ezekiel 45 describes an ideal order for the restored people: a portion of the land is separated for the LORD, for the priests, the Levites, the city and prince; the civil power is corrected not to oppress; and the worship is reorganized with offerings and feasts turned to the purification of the house of God and the people. The chapter unites holiness, justice, and worship: the earth belongs to God, the rulers must serve without exploitation, and the worship must be sustained with honest measures and regular sacrifices. In an evangelical perspective, this points to a people of God ordained according to the divine presence, ethical righteousness and the continuous need for atonement.

outline.title: The holy portion on earth and the distribution among priests, Levites, city and prince
outline.explanation: The first verses delimit a separate space for the sanctuary and for the ministers of worship. The text insists that the center of the people's life is the presence of God, and not just the possession of the earth. The division also protects priests, Levites and the city, while restricting the power of the prince so that he does not oppress the people.

outline.title: Justice in the measures and responsibility of the prince before the people
outline.explanation: The Lord commands the princes to stop violence and oppression and to wear correct scales, ephas and battle. The offerings of the people are organized accurately, and the prince appears as responsible for conducting the offerings in the solemnities, new moons, Saturdays and feasts, making atonement for the house of Israel. Worship and public life are treated as inseparable realities.

outline.title: Purification of the sanctuary and feasts of atonement in the first and seventh months
outline.explanation: The chapter ends with rites of purification at the beginning of the year, then with the Passover, and finally with the feast of the seventh month, in which the prince offers sacrifices similar to those of the passover. The highlight lies on the continuous need for ritual cleansing, atonement and fidelity in the cult along the sacred calendar.

study.context: The chapter is part of Ezekiel's final view of a restored community. The given notes place the text as an arrangement for the people after exile, with the land divided in order to centralize the sanctuary. They also indicate that this drawing is not limited to a simple agricultural division, but emphasizes that the land should remind the people that God dwells in the midst of it. The text uses language of vision and cultual order, and the commentator notes relate it to the return of the people and, in confessional reading, to the broader and purest character of the covenant community.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter states that the earth, leadership and worship belong to the Lord. The holy portion recalls that the presence of God comes before human possession; therefore, space is organized from the sanctuary. The condemnation of oppression shows that social justice is not a secondary matter, but part of fidelity to God. The correct measures teach honesty in economic relations. The offerings and feasts show that sin continues to be serious and that reconciliation with God requires purification, atonement, and ordained worship. In evangelical reading, this underscores the need for a holy people, righteous rulers and cult centered on divine holiness, without suggesting that the structure described be copied mechanically outside its visionary context.

scholarViews.insight: The first portion of the earth is separated as a holy portion of the LORD, not only for just division, but to remember that the promised land exists for the dwelling of God in the midst of his people.
The text sends that princes and people observe distributive and commutative justice; piety without honesty does not please God or benefit the people.
The feast of the seventh month must repeat, by the prince, the same acts prescribed for the Passover, with the same kind of sacrifices and ceremonies.

questions: What changes in our reading of the earth, resources and leadership when we remember that everything must be before the Lord?
In what ways can the church unite holiness in worship and practical justice in economic and power relations?
How does the need for atonement and purification in this chapter help to understand the seriousness of sin and the grace of God?
study.practice: Examine whether your life treats God as a centre or as an appendix. Practice honesty in finance, words and decisions, refusing any advantage gained by oppression or manipulation. In worship and daily life, value the confession of sins, reverence and the continual dependence on God's mercy. If you exercise any leadership, use it to serve, not to explore. If you do not lead, support a community marked by justice and holiness with prayer and responsibility.
study.uncertainty: This chapter is presented in the form of prophetic vision, and the notes provided allow various theological readings about its final application. There is also a textual limitation in the notes on the seventh month feast: the commentaries mention that the celebration is not explicitly named in Hebrew, although the interpretive tradition associates it with the Feast of Tabernacles; here this was treated as interpretation, not as absolute certainty of the text.
